title: Agentic frameworks for software engineering
big_idea: Code is the easiest place to self-improve because the computer grades the work: tests pass or fail, and code runs faster or slower. Sample many attempts, let tests (even model-written ones) pick the winner, and give the agent clear feedback from the system, such as a profiler, instead of a bare number.

papers.title: CodeMonkeys: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Software Engineering
papers.what: A SWE-bench system in three steps: find relevant files (a cheap model scans every file), generate 10 parallel multi-turn attempts that each write a code edit and a test script and iterate on execution feedback, then select by running all model-written tests on all edits, keeping the top 3 by votes, and letting a model (which can write more tests) choose.
papers.result: 57.4% of SWE-bench Verified resolved for about 2,300 USD, with 69.8% coverage (some attempt was correct). Selecting over an ensemble of edits from top leaderboard submissions reached 66.2%, above the best single member (62.8%). Different splits between serial and parallel compute often gave similar coverage. Model selection without the top-3 vote filter did worse than plain voting; with the filter it did better.
papers.takeaway: Treat generation and selection as separate problems and measure both (coverage vs final score). Cheap test-based voting to cut the pool, then a model judge on the short list, closes much of the gap.

papers.title: KernelBench: Can LLMs Write Efficient GPU Kernels?
papers.what: 250 PyTorch workloads in three levels. The model rewrites each as faster GPU code. Outputs are compared with the reference on 5 random inputs and both are timed. The metric fast_p is the fraction of tasks that are correct and faster than the reference by more than a factor p.
papers.result: One-shot, frontier reasoning models matched the PyTorch baseline in fewer than 20% of cases. With execution and profiler feedback over 10 refinement turns, the paper reports fast_1 rising from 12%, 36% and 12% to 43%, 72% and 18% across the three levels (the paper's Table 1 lists 2% as the Level 3 starting value; its introduction says 12%); the headline case is DeepSeek-R1 on Level 2, from 36% to 72%. Execution feedback mostly fixed execution errors; functional correctness stayed hard.
papers.takeaway: Grade speed and correctness together with one number (fast_p), check on several random inputs, and feed the model real execution and profiling output each turn.

papers.title: Improving Parallel Program Performance with LLM Optimizers via Agent-System Interfaces
papers.what: An LLM optimizer (via the Trace framework, with GPT-4o) writes mappers that decide where tasks and data go in parallel programs. The agent-system interface has a small domain-specific language that hides low-level C++ and defines the search space, and AutoGuide, which turns raw execution output into explanations and suggested changes.
papers.result: Within 10 iterations it beat OpenTuner run for 1000 iterations, by 3.8x. Its mappers beat expert-written ones by up to 1.34x across nine benchmarks, cutting tuning from days to minutes. The DSL gave much higher code-generation success than raw C++.
papers.takeaway: Design what the agent sees and writes. A narrow action language plus feedback that explains errors and suggests fixes can matter more than a bigger model or more iterations.

terms: Fraction of problems where at least one generated attempt is correct; the best any selector can do.
Serial: more turns of fixing one attempt. Parallel: more independent attempts.
Run every model-written test on every candidate edit; the edit that passes the most tests wins.
Fraction of tasks where the new code is correct AND more than p times faster than the reference; fast_0 is plain correctness.
The layer between the agent and the system: what actions the agent can write and what feedback it gets back.
A step that turns raw system output (errors, timings) into plain explanations and suggested changes for the agent.
A tool that reports which functions used the most time; Python's built-in one is cProfile.
traps: High coverage is not a high score. More parallel samples can make selection harder.
Model-written tests can be wrong. Drop tests that already pass on the buggy code, and don't trust a single test.
A model judge on the whole pool can do worse than plain voting; filter to a short list first.
Checking speed on one input invites gaming. Check correctness on several random inputs, including edge cases like large values.
A speedup threshold of 1x is easy when the baseline is a Python loop and hard when the baseline is already tuned. Pick p for your baseline.
Timing is noisy. Take the best of several runs and keep timing in a separate process.
Never run model-written code in your own process. Use a subprocess with a timeout and a fresh folder.
check: Context (find relevant files), generation (sample edits and tests), and selection (choose one edit).
How does CodeMonkeys select an edit?
It runs model-written tests on all edits, keeps the top 3 by votes, and a model picks among them, optionally writing more tests.
The fraction of tasks where the generated code is correct and faster than the reference.
What did profiler and execution feedback do for DeepSeek-R1 on KernelBench Level 2?
Raised fast_1 from 36% to 72% over 10 turns of refinement.
What are the two parts of the agent-system interface in Wei et al.?
A domain-specific language for mappers, and AutoGuide, which turns raw execution output into actionable feedback.
